\chapter{Five Things on a Plate}
\label{ch:la-harina-y-la-uva}
\hlchaptermodality{376}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la harina, la uva, el maíz, el chocolate and el pimiento, and name five things that go on a plate.}

Complete ES-C376-pimiento: name five things that go on a plate, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la harina]{la harina — the f that turned into silence}

\label{lesson:ES-C376-harina}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the kiss}, then \emph{the nephew}. (\emph{El beso}; \emph{El sobrino}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pan — what it becomes.
  \item el trigo — what it was first.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-RI-na}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{h} is written and not pronounced, so the word opens on its vowel. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la harina} — \textquotedblleft{}flour.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{farīna} was ground grain, built on \textbf{far} — husked wheat, the coarse stuff Romans ate long before anybody bolted flour fine. English holds the same Latin word twice, in \textbf{farina} and \textbf{farinaceous}.

Spanish turned the \textbf{f} into an \textbf{h}, and then stopped pronouncing the \emph{h} altogether. You have already met the change several times without it being named:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{facere} $\to$ \textbf{hacer};
  \item \emph{filius} $\to$ \textbf{hijo};
  \item \emph{farīna} $\to$ \textbf{harina}.
\end{itemize}

Here is the part that makes it usable rather than a curiosity. The change had a \textbf{boundary}. It did not happen before \emph{r}, before \emph{l}, or before the \emph{ue} glide, which is why these kept their \emph{f}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{frente}, not \emph{hrente};
  \item \textbf{flor}, not \emph{hlor};
  \item \textbf{fuego}, not \emph{huego}.
\end{itemize}

Do not turn that into a rule about every \emph{f}, though, because there is a second reason and it covers many more words: \textbf{the word never went through the change at all.} It was lifted out of written Latin centuries after the change had finished, so there was nothing for it to apply to. \emph{Fácil}, \emph{familia}, \emph{forma}, \emph{final}, \emph{fecha}, \emph{feliz} and \emph{fiesta} are all in that group.

So an initial \emph{f} tells you one of two things. Either an \emph{r}, an \emph{l} or a \emph{ue} was standing directly behind it -- or the word came into Spanish through a book rather than through speech.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what bread is made of: \emph{la harina}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la harina}
  \item \emph{un kilo de harina}
  \item \emph{harina y agua}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happened to the \emph{f} of Latin \emph{farīna}? (It became a written, silent \emph{h}.) And name the two reasons a Spanish word can still start with \emph{f}. (An \emph{r}, \emph{l} or \emph{ue} stood behind it — or it was lifted from written Latin long after the change finished.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la uva]{la uva — a little grape in your throat}

\label{lesson:ES-C376-uva}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the nephew}, then \emph{the flour}. (\emph{El sobrino}; \emph{La harina}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el vino — what it becomes.
  \item la fruta — the family it belongs to.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{U-va}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{v} is the same sound as a soft \emph{b}, made with the lips barely touching. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la uva} — \textquotedblleft{}grape.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{uva} meant a grape — and also the bunch. One word for the single thing and the cluster, which is convenient when the two rarely appear apart.

Its diminutive was \textbf{uvula}, \textquotedblleft{}little grape,\textquotedblright{} and that word is still in English, unchanged, naming the small soft flap that hangs at the back of your throat.

Why that name? Because whoever first wrote it down thought the flap looked like a small grape, and said so. That is worth pausing on. Most of the time an explanation of why a word means what it does has to be reconstructed, and reconstructions can be talked into almost anything. Here the reason was written down at the time.

So you have a Spanish fruit and an English piece of anatomy that are the same Latin word, one of them shrunk, and a recorded explanation joining them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what wine starts as: \emph{la uva}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la uva}
  \item \emph{las uvas}
  \item \emph{un kilo de uvas}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{uva} cover, one grape or the bunch? (Both.) And what is the \emph{uvula} named after? (A little grape, because of how it looks.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el maíz]{el maíz — one of the first words to cross}

\label{lesson:ES-C376-maiz}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the flour}, then \emph{the grape}. (\emph{La harina}; \emph{La uva}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el trigo — the grain Europe already had.
  \item la patata — another word that came the same way.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-ÍZ}, two beats with the weight on the second. The written accent on the \emph{í} keeps the \emph{a} and the \emph{i} apart, so they do not collapse into one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el maíz} — \textquotedblleft{}maize.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Maíz} comes from \textbf{mahís}, a word in Taíno — the Arawakan language spoken in the Caribbean islands Columbus reached in 1492. Spanish took it and handed it on: English \textbf{maize} is the Spanish word with an English spelling.

It was among the very first American words to reach Europe. \emph{Canoa} is in the same log, recorded within a fortnight of landfall, and so are \emph{hamaca} and \emph{cacique}.

A note on how to say that safely. It is tempting to promote \emph{maíz} to \textbf{the} first — a good line, and unprovable. Which word arrived first depends on which manuscript you trust and which transcription of it, and \emph{canoa} is the usual claimant anyway. \textquotedblleft{}Among the first\textquotedblright{} is a claim the evidence supports. \textquotedblleft{}The first\textquotedblright{} is a claim nobody can check, and this word does not need it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name a grain that crossed an ocean: \emph{el maíz}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el maíz}
  \item \emph{un poco de maíz}
  \item \emph{harina de maíz}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language did \emph{maíz} come from? (Taíno, in the Caribbean.) And which word probably reached Europe before it? (\emph{Canoa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el chocolate]{el chocolate — a famous etymology that is not attested}

\label{lesson:ES-C376-chocolate}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the grape}, then \emph{the maize}. (\emph{La uva}; \emph{El maíz}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la leche — what it is usually made with.
  \item el azúcar — what was added later.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cho-co-LA-te}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in English \emph{church}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el chocolate} — \textquotedblleft{}chocolate.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Chocolate} came into Spanish from \textbf{Nahuatl}, the language of the Aztec empire. That much is agreed.

After that, very little is. The Academy's dictionary marks the entry \textbf{disputed} — which a dictionary does not do lightly.

You have probably met the standard story: Nahuatl \textbf{xocolātl}, \textquotedblleft{}bitter water,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{xoco} \textquotedblleft{}bitter\textquotedblright{} and \emph{atl} \textquotedblleft{}water.\textquotedblright{} It has a problem. \textbf{No colonial source records that word.} It is missing from Molina's dictionary, the great sixteenth-century record of the language, and \emph{chocolatl} does not surface in Nahuatl until the seventeen hundreds — long after the drink was being drunk in Madrid.

And notice the shape of the argument. \textquotedblleft{}Bitter water\textquotedblright{} is not evidence for the etymology; it is the etymology chopped in half and read back. Segmenting a reconstruction and then admiring how well the pieces fit proves only that you did the segmenting.

The proposal that has gained ground instead is \textbf{chicolātl}, from \textbf{chicolli} — the wooden stick used to beat the drink into foam. The drink named for the implement, not the taste. Two things support it: living Nahuatl dialects, and the \textbf{i} that shows up in the earliest borrowings outside Spanish, where \textquotedblleft{}bitter water\textquotedblright{} predicts an \emph{o}.

So this is a word you can use with complete confidence and cannot explain with any.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what was drunk before it was eaten: \emph{el chocolate}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el chocolate}
  \item \emph{un chocolate}
  \item \emph{chocolate con leche}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Academy's dictionary say about this etymology? (That it is disputed.) And what does the leading proposal name the drink after? (\emph{Chicolli}, the stick used to whisk it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pimiento]{el pimiento — a name that arrived through the spice cupboard}

\label{lesson:ES-C376-pimiento}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the maize}, then \emph{the chocolate}. (\emph{El maíz}; \emph{El chocolate}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la sal — the other thing on every table.
  \item el tomate — another that crossed the same ocean.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pi-MIEN-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{ie} is one glide, not two separate vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pimiento} — \textquotedblleft{}pepper.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Pimiento} comes from \textbf{pimienta}, black pepper, and \emph{pimienta} is Latin \textbf{pigmenta} — the plural of \textbf{pigmentum}.

A \emph{pigmentum} started out as colouring matter, the stuff a painter grinds. In later Latin it slid: from colouring matter to \textbf{a drug}, from a drug to \textbf{an ingredient}, from an ingredient to \textbf{a condiment}. And the condiment that mattered most in medieval Europe was pepper. So a word that began in the paint pot ended up meaning the spice.

It is tempting to shorten that to \textquotedblleft{}the pepper is named for its colour.\textquotedblright{} Do not. That version takes the \emph{earliest} sense of the Latin word, skips the three steps that actually carried it, and then points at a red pepper as though the colour were the proof. The dictionary's own gloss lays the route out, and the route runs through the apothecary, not the paint.

English keeps the older sense alive in \textbf{pigment}, and \textbf{paint} is a relative — both are built on \emph{pingere}, \textquotedblleft{}to paint.\textquotedblright{}

One more turn. The pepper on a Spanish table is American, and it was named by transfer: Europeans reached for the word they already had for the hot thing you grind. \emph{Pimienta} stayed with the peppercorn; \emph{pimiento} went to the newcomer.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name a pepper: \emph{un pimiento}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pimiento}
  \item \emph{un pimiento}
  \item \emph{un pimiento rojo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{pigmentum} come to mean by late Latin? (A drug, an ingredient, a condiment.) And was the pepper named for its colour? (No — for being the spice.)
\end{tcolorbox}
